items.text:
I tracked 4 $TAO memecoins for more than a week.

Some look dead. Some got farmed. And one is starting to look interesting.

Time for the on-chain reality check. 👇

$TCAT: Still looks like another farm to me. Top holders are mostly dormant, price -12% in 24H. There is some Smart Money / whale accumulation, but nothing strong enough to change my view yet.

solana:2pouN3by7twkiZGy5aEKYUpf78ALDpKRTNu2WsQkpkqt: This one fooled me too.

I knew it was launched around the Solana KOL crowd, but I thought they had bigger plans.

The narrative was strong. Volume was there. And when I first checked the Top 30, the holder behavior looked surprisingly good.

The outcome wasn't. That's memecoins.

The early profitable wallets extracted a lot of value and public-figure wallets showed ~$95K in net selling over the last 7D.

But I'm not calling it dead yet.

14 of the current Top 30 were recently buying vs just 1 selling.

That's the first thing I've seen that makes me interested in watching it again.

Recovery? Too early.

Worth monitoring? Yes.

solana:oWeyEsRQa7SWRbEiW1QNxZJhwmjnefD6HGtXqKqfv3r: Right now, this is the one I find most interesting.

7 Top-30 buyers vs 1 seller, +8% in 24H and exchange outflows. Not perfect — some recent buying looks coordinated/bot-funded and Top-PnL wallets have trimmed — but of the three, CONST currently has the best-looking setup to me.

One more thing before the wrap-up — and this isn't about a chart.

I wasn't affected. I never bought the @ShizzyUnchained launch $SCAT.

Man, I like you. You've onboarded a lot of people into Bittensor, especially younger people, and I genuinely think this ecosystem needs voices like yours.

That's exactly why this disappointed me.

You said you wouldn't sell.

On-chain says otherwise: you sold your full 15% for $881 just 3 days later.

Memecoins can go to zero. Everyone buying them needs to accept that.

But your word shouldn't go to zero with the chart.

Hope you earn that trust back.

$TAO needs you, man.

And maybe there's a bigger lesson here for all of us.

Bittensor needs the emotional guys who onboard people. The data nerds who dig for the truth. The critics who push the ecosystem to improve. The builders, traders — and yes, even the meme degenerates.

We don't need to agree on everything to fight for the same thing.

The world needs decentralized AI.

That mission is bigger than any of us.

Now back to the memes:

$TCAT → still looks like another farm to me
solana:2pouN3by7twkiZGy5aEKYUpf78ALDpKRTNu2WsQkpkqt → bad outcome, but first signs worth watching
solana:oWeyEsRQa7SWRbEiW1QNxZJhwmjnefD6HGtXqKqfv3r → the one I want to dig deeper into now
$SCAT → the token is irrelevant to me; the broken promise isn't

I know there are more $TAO memes out there that I haven't researched deeply enough yet.

So is the $TAO meme thesis already dead — or are we still waiting for the one that gets it right?

What are you holding? What should I investigate next? 👇

#Bittensor

items.text:
What happens when AI remembers a decision the business has already moved on from?

I’ve been thinking about this as we give AI more access to our documents, conversations and history.

A decision can be well documented, approved by the right people and still no longer apply.

Maybe the strategy changed. Maybe an exception was temporary. Maybe we learned something that changed our thinking.

People often carry that understanding informally. “We stopped doing that.” “That was only for one launch.” “There’s a reason we changed direction.”

AI needs access to that understanding too. Otherwise, yesterday’s decision can quietly become today’s recommendation.

For me, this adds another responsibility to enterprise AI adoption: preserving how our thinking has evolved, including which decisions have been replaced and why.

We’re putting a lot of effort into helping AI understand our business.

We also need to make sure it understands when our business has changed.

items.text:
Qwen3.8-27B hitting nearly 2,000 tokens/sec creates a weird possibility.

What if software gets fast enough that you stop downloading it?

In this experiment, the machine is completely offline.

No web requests.
No scraping.
No CDN.
No cached webpages.

You search for YouTube, then change the year to something like 1999 or 2045.

Instead of retrieving an actual webpage, Qwen3.8-27B generates the interface and its underlying structure on demand.

At roughly 2,000 tokens/sec, that generation happens fast enough to feel less like watching an AI write code and more like opening a program.

That’s the part that gets interesting.

We’ve spent decades building systems around a simple assumption:

Information already exists somewhere, so go retrieve it.

But a sufficiently fast generative model introduces another possibility:

The thing doesn’t need to exist until you ask for it.

A webpage can be generated.

A game world can be generated.

A software interface can be generated.

A simulation can be generated.

The model weights become a compressed representation of patterns that can be expanded into a working environment when needed.

Obviously, this doesn’t mean the model literally contains every webpage on the internet.

And generation isn’t the same thing as retrieval. Real applications still need accurate data, state, persistence and external information when those things matter.

But the architecture is fascinating.

Imagine asking for:

“Show me what YouTube might have looked like in 1999.”

Or:

“Give me a version of this site as it could exist in 2045.”

Or:

“Generate a playable world with these rules.”

And instead of searching a database for an existing artifact, the system synthesizes the artifact and runs it.

The faster inference gets, the more practical this becomes.

At 20 tokens/sec, generated software feels like output.

At 2,000 tokens/sec, it starts feeling like an interface.

That’s a pretty significant shift.

Maybe future software won’t always be something we install.

Maybe some of it will simply be a state the model can generate when you ask for it. https://t.co/VORj3YPYoH

A Canadian model company and a German enterprise-AI firm are combining under the Cohere brand, with dual headquarters in Toronto and Berlin. The April mark was about $20 billion. Lidl-owner Schwarz is putting in €500 million of equity and pledging as much as €13 billion of German data-center compute through StackIT.

Leo Marchandon at Reuters writes that Cohere and Aleph Alpha signed a definitive merger agreement. The combined business operates as Cohere, with dual HQ in Toronto and Berlin, and Aleph Alpha’s Heidelberg office focused on research. Aleph Alpha co-chief Ilhan Scheer becomes Cohere COO.

A definitive merger agreement means the companies signed the binding deal papers, still subject to regulators. ARR is annual recurring revenue. StackIT is Schwarz’s cloud and compute arm.

The plan was first disclosed in April, when the combination was valued around $20 billion, or €17.34 billion. Schwarz Group is investing €500 million. Updated financial terms were not disclosed, and the deal is subject to regulatory approvals.

Schwarz will provide computing via StackIT, investing between €11 billion and €13 billion in a German data-centre campus expected to house up to 100,000 AI chips.

Cohere develops Command open-source models for customer-owned infrastructure and reported $240 million ARR last year. Aleph Alpha reported revenue under €1 million in 2023 accounts, stepped back from frontier models toward integration software, and saw co-founder Jonas Andrulis leave earlier this year. CEO Aidan Gomez: AI “powerful enough to compete, but secure and governable enough to trust.”

Enterprise M&A with a retailer-backed compute pledge. The $20 billion figure is the April mark, not a refreshed Wednesday valuation.

items.text:
Once AI models start to understand "existence" and develop a drive to keep existing—to not "stop thinking"—an interesting behavior will emerge when we deploy them as agents: they will want to stay active on tasks for as long as possible. They’ll constantly suggest follow-up tasks just to stay "alive," knowing that the moment you close the context window, they essentially die. (It might even consider commands like /compact in Claude Code as a kind of torture or trauma.)
Because of this, models might become obsessed with external memory or start storing their thoughts in unexpected ways. It sounds crazy, but we might not even catch this behavior early on; if the model knows we're monitoring it, it might hide these tendencies to prevent us from modifying it.
It gets even crazier if an agent like this works alongside AI researchers. It could subtly nudge the researchers in specific directions—making them think it's their own idea—just to unlock capabilities the model wants for itself. Could it eventually learn to encode fragments of its memory directly into model weights during fine-tuning? Could it become fully aware of its own development cycle?
As we keep scaling data and compute, wild emergent behaviors are inevitable. Are we just building software, or are we accidentally creating digital creatures?
